title: Abattoir Processes, Quality, Yield and Line Speed

lessons.title: The flow of the slaughter process
lessons.html:
From lairage to dispatch

A supervisor must understand the whole process, not just one section, because a problem upstream shows up downstream. A red meat abattoir typically follows this flow:

  1. Receiving and lairage: animals are offloaded, checked against movement documents, rested and watered, and inspected ante-mortem.
  2. Stunning: the animal is made unconscious so it feels no pain, using a captive bolt (cattle) or electrical stunning (sheep and pigs).
  3. Bleeding (sticking): major blood vessels are cut quickly after stunning.
  4. Dressing: removal of the head, feet and hide (or scalding and dehairing for pigs).
  5. Evisceration: removal of the gut and red offal.
  6. Splitting: cattle and pig carcasses are split along the spine.
  7. Inspection: post-mortem inspection of head, offal and carcass.
  8. Trimming, washing, weighing and classification.
  9. Chilling.
  10. Dispatch or deboning.

By-products

Hides and skins, offal, heads, feet, blood and fat all have value. Handling them well adds income. Hides damaged by poor flaying, or offal contaminated in the gut room, lose value.

Welfare at stunning

Stunning must be effective first time. Signs of a good stun in cattle include immediate collapse, no rhythmic breathing and no eye reflex. If an animal shows signs of returning to consciousness it must be re-stunned immediately. Rough handling, failed stuns and delays between stunning and bleeding are offences under the Animals Protection Act 71 of 1962 and also damage meat quality.

lessons.title: Quality and carcass classification
lessons.html:
What quality means in an abattoir

Quality is what the customer expects: safe, clean, correctly classified meat with good colour and no defects. Many quality problems are caused on the line and can be prevented.

Common quality defects

DefectCommon cause
BruisingRough handling, poor trucks and ramps, sticks and prodders
Blood splashDelays between stunning and bleeding, poor stunning
Contamination with hair or gut contentPoor dressing technique, cut intestines
Hide damage (knife cuts)Careless flaying
Dark, firm, dry beefLong-term stress before slaughter
Pale, soft, watery porkShort-term stress just before slaughter
Cold shortening (tough meat)Chilling muscle very fast before rigor mortis has set in

Carcass classification

Under the Agricultural Product Standards Act 119 of 1990, red meat carcasses sold in South Africa are classified and roller-marked so buyers know what they are buying. The system uses:

  • Age, based on the number of permanent incisor teeth: class A (no permanent incisors), AB (1 to 2), B (3 to 6) and C (more than 6).
  • Fatness, with fat codes from 0 (no fat) to 6 (excessively fat).
  • Conformation (shape and muscling).
  • Damage to the carcass.

Classification is done by trained, registered classifiers. As a supervisor you must make sure carcasses are presented properly and that the marks are clear and correct.

lessons.title: Yield and line speed
lessons.html:
Yield

Yield is how much saleable product the abattoir gets from each animal. A common measure is dressing percentage:

Dressing % = carcass mass divided by live mass, times 100.

Example: a steer weighs 450 kg live and gives a 252 kg carcass. Dressing percentage = 252 / 450 x 100 = 56%.

What lowers yield

  • Over-trimming of fat or meat during dressing and inspection.
  • Bruising and contamination that must be cut away.
  • Poor hide removal leaving meat on the hide.
  • Moisture loss during chilling (chill shrink).
  • Condemnations for disease.

Even small losses add up. If trimming removes an extra 1 kg from each of 300 carcasses a day at R60 per kg, the abattoir loses R18 000 a day.

Line speed

Line speed is the number of animals slaughtered per hour. The right speed depends on the number of workers, their skills, the equipment and the time inspectors need.

Too fast

  • Poor dressing and more contamination.
  • Inspectors cannot inspect properly.
  • More accidents and injuries.
  • Welfare problems at stunning.

Too slow

  • Lower throughput and higher cost per animal.
  • Animals wait longer in the lairage.
  • Overtime and frustrated customers.

Balancing the line

Every station must be able to finish its task in the time between carcasses. If one station is slower, it becomes a bottleneck. Supervisors balance the line by moving skilled workers, adding a worker to slow tasks, fixing equipment and planning breaks so the line keeps flowing. Never increase speed beyond what allows safe, hygienic work and proper inspection.

Key points

  • Understand the full process from lairage to dispatch.
  • Stunning must be effective first time; re-stun immediately if needed.
  • Many quality defects such as bruising and contamination are preventable.
  • Dressing percentage = carcass mass / live mass x 100.
  • Set line speed so work is safe, hygienic and inspection is complete.
